answer.text:
This is two $LC$ oscillators coupled to each other.

Put $V_{1}=X_{1}-Y_{1}$ , $V_{2}=X_{2}-Y_{2}$ for
the differential voltages. Let per side

$$ Y_{p}= G_{p}+jB $$

$$ G_{p}=1/R_{p}\;\;,\;\; B=\omega C-\frac1{\omega L} $$

be the tank admittance to ac ground. $L$ is the
physical inductor, $C$ is the total capacitance
to ground on $X_{1},Y_{1},X_{2},Y_{2}$,
explicit plus

* $C_{DB}$ of the core device and of the coupling device,
* $C_{gd}$ with Miller,
* $C_{gs}$ of the opposite core gate and of the
driven coupling gate of the other core,
* inductor and wiring parasitics.

Let $g_{SS}$ be the small signal $g_{m}$ of the
core cross coupled devices, tail $I_{SS}$,
$g_{1}$ that of the coupling devices, tail $I_{1}$.

E.g. for the upper core, drains on $X_{1},Y_{1}$,

* $M_{2},M_{3}$ : cross coupled, gates $Y_{1},X_{1}$,
  sources to $I_{SS}$,
* $M_{1},M_{4}$ : coupling pair, drains $X_{1},Y_{1}$,
  sources to $I_{1}$, gates driven by the other
  oscillator.

With virtual earth on the common sources,
for the upper oscillator KCL on $X_{1}$ and $Y_{1}$
gives, differentially,

$$ V_{X1}Y_{p}+i_{D1}+i_{D2}=0 $$
$$ V_{Y1}Y_{p}+i_{D4}+i_{D3}=0 $$

Subtract. $i_{D2}-i_{D3}$ is the cross-coupled
pair:

$$ i_{D2}=g_{SS}V_{Y1}\;,\;i_{D3}=g_{SS}V_{X1} $$

in small signal with $V_{s}=0$, i.e.

$$ i_{D2}-i_{D3}=-g_{SS}V_{1} .$$

$i_{D1}-i_{D4}$ is the coupling pair driven
by $V_{2}$:

$$ i_{D1}-i_{D4}=g_{1}(V_{G1}-V_{G4}) .$$

With the wiring shown one coupling is straight,
the other is crossed. I.e. to within an overall
sign

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{G1}-V_{G4}|_{up} &= -V_{2} \\
V_{G1}-V_{G4}|_{low} &= +V_{1}
\end{aligned}$$

Hence differentially

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{1}(Y_{p}-g_{SS})-g_{1}V_{2}&=0 \\
V_{2}(Y_{p}-g_{SS})+g_{1}V_{1}&=0
\end{aligned}\tag{1}$$

Put $A=Y_{p}-g_{SS}$, $B=g_{1}$. Then

$$\det \begin{bmatrix}A & -B \\ B & A\end{bmatrix}
 =A^{2}+B^{2}=0 $$

i.e.

$$ Y_{p}-g_{SS}= \pm jg_{1}. \tag{2}$$

In particular $|V_{1}|=|V_{2}|$ and from (1)

$$ \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} = \pm j $$

the two tanks oscillate in quadrature.

Eq.2 is the Barkhausen condition. In real part,

$$ G_{p}-G_{SS}=0 $$

in steady state, $G_{SS}$ compressed to cancel
tank loss, as usual. In imaginary part

$$ B = \omega C-\frac{1}{\omega L}= \pm G_{1} \tag{3}$$

where $G_{1}$ is the large signal effective $g_{1}$
at the fundamental. The quadrature injection current
$\pm jG_{1}V$ looks like a susceptance in parallel
with the tank and pulls the tank off resonance.

I.e.

$$ C\omega^{2}\mp G_{1}\omega-\frac1L=0 $$

$$ \omega =\frac{\pm G_{1}+\sqrt{G_{1}^{2}+4C/L}}{2C}. $$

For weak coupling, $G_{1}\ll \sqrt{C/L}= \omega_{0}C$,

$$ B\approx 2C\,\Delta\omega $$

$$ \Delta\omega \approx \pm \frac{G_{1}}{2C}. $$

To first order this is the free tank resonance

$$ \omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}= \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} $$

$$f_{osc}\approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$

per side $L,C$, the two cores in quadrature.
The $\pm G_{1}/2C$ is the quadrature pulling,
normally $\ll\omega_{0}$ for high $Q$.

It does not state the required coupling fraction in the αω0/(2Q) form or an equivalent normalized ratio, so it misses the general frequency-shift estimate.

answer.text:
The 4 inductors with the capacitance at $X_{1},Y_{1},
X_{2},Y_{2}$ form two nominally identical differential
$LC$ tanks.

* Top: $L$ at $X_{1},Y_{1}$, core $X$-pair $T_{2},T_{3}$
with tail $I_{SS}$, coupling pair $T_{1},T_{4}$ with
tail $I_{1}$.
* Bottom: $L$ at $X_{2},Y_{2}$, core $X$-pair with
tail $I_{SS}$, coupling pair with tail $I_{1}$.

The drains of core and coupling are in parallel on
the local tank. The gates of the core are cross
connected to the local tank. The gates of the
coupling pair are driven differentially by the
other tank, once straight and once crossed. This
is the parallel quadrature $LC$ oscillator.

Put for one side single ended tank admittance

$$Y_{0}= \frac1{R_{p}}+j\Bigl(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\Bigr) $$

$C$ = total to ground at $X,Y$, $R_{p}$ = parallel
loss, 
$$\omega_{0}^{2}=\frac1{LC}\;,\qquad 
Q =\frac{R_{p}}{L\omega_{0}}=\omega_{0}CR_{p} .$$

Let in differential operation

$$V_{Y1}=-V_{X1},\qquad V_{Y2}=-V_{X2} .$$

Put $V_{X1}=V_{1}$, $V_{X2}=V_{2}$.
With straight coupling on top and crossed on
bottom, KCL at e.g. $X_{1},X_{2}$, in small
signal with transistor $g_{m0}$ for the core,
$g_{m1}$ for the coupling, source nodes virtual
ground,

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{1}Y_{0}+g_{m0}V_{Y1}+g_{m1}V_{2}&=0\\
V_{2}Y_{0}+g_{m0}V_{Y2}-g_{m1}V_{1}&=0
\end{aligned}$$

i.e.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{1}(Y_{0}-g_{m0})+g_{m1}V_{2}&=0\\
 -g_{m1}V_{1}+V_{2}(Y_{0}-g_{m0})&=0 .
\end{aligned}$$

Non-trivial $V_{1},V_{2}$ requires

$$\det = (Y_{0}-g_{m0})^{2}+g_{m1}^{2}=0,$$

$$Y_{0}=g_{m0}\pm jg_{m1}. \tag{1}$$

Hence

$$\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} = \mp j,$$

i.e. the two differential outputs

$$V_{d1}=V_{X1}-V_{Y1},\quad V_{d2}=V_{X2}-V_{Y2}$$

are in quadrature. $V_{d2}$ lags or leads $V_{d1}$
by $90^{\circ}$ according to the $\pm$ sign.

Eq.1 says the active circuit looks like $-g_{m0}$
in parallel with $\mp jg_{m1}$. The quadrature
injected current is $90^{\circ}$ away, so to first
order it contributes only susceptance. The tank
must provide the opposite susceptance. I.e. with

$$Y_{0}=G_{p}+jB,\; G_{p}=1/R_{p},\;
B=\omega C-1/\omega L,$$

$$\begin{aligned}
G_{p} &= g_{m0}\\
B &= \pm g_{m1} .
\end{aligned}\tag{2}$$

Start up needs $g_{m0}>G_{p}$. In steady state
$g_{m0},g_{m1}$ compress to satisfy (2).

In large signal the pairs switch the tail currents.
The fundamental of the square-wave single-ended
current is $\propto I_{tail}$. The core injects
$\propto I_{SS}$ in phase with the local voltage,
the coupling injects $\propto I_{1}$ in quadrature.
Hence the effective

$$\frac{B}{G_{p}} = \pm \frac{I_{c1}}{I_{c0}}
 \approx \pm \frac{I_{1}}{I_{SS}} .$$

I.e.

$$R_{p}\Bigl(\omega_{osc}C-\frac1{\omega_{osc}L}\Bigr)
 =\pm \frac{I_{1}}{I_{SS}}. \tag{3}$$

Near resonance

$$R_{p}\Bigl(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\Bigr)
 \approx 2Q\frac{\omega-\omega_{0}}{\omega_{0}} .$$

Hence two quadrature modes, above and below
resonance,

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}\pm 
\frac{\omega_{0}}{2Q}\frac{I_{1}}{I_{SS}} $$

$$ =\omega_{0}\pm \frac{1}{2R_{p}C}\frac{I_{1}}{I_{SS}} .$$

In particular for weak coupling and/or high $Q$,

$$ \omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}= \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} $$

with $(X_{1}-Y_{1})$ $90^{\circ}$ from
$(X_{2}-Y_{2})$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly starts from the tank resonance and derives the coupling-induced shift as approximately ±(I1/ISS)·ω0/(2Q), matching the required estimate. The two possible quadrature modes and the weak-coupling limit are also stated.

answer.text:
This is two $LC$ oscillators coupled to each other
so as to oscillate in quadrature.

Call the upper oscillator 1 and the lower 2.
Put

$$V_{1}=X_{1}-Y_{1}\;,\qquad V_{2}=X_{2}-Y_{2}$$

in the small signal sense.

$L$ to $V_{DD}$ is $sL$ to ac ground.
Let $C$ be the total capacitance to ground at
$X_{1},Y_{1},X_{2},Y_{2}$, i.e. inductor
capacitance plus wiring plus

* $C_{db}$ of the drain that lives on the node,
* $C_{gs}$ plus Millered $C_{gd}$ of the gates
  driven by the node.

In oscillator 1 the middle pair is the normal
cross coupled pair. Drains on $X_{1},Y_{1}$,
gates on $Y_{1},X_{1}$, tail $I_{SS}$.
Let its $g_{m}$ be $g_{SS}$.

The outer pair is the coupling pair.
Drains on $X_{1},Y_{1}$, tail $I_{1}$.
Let its $g_{m}$ be $g_{1}$. Its gates are
driven by oscillator 2. Similarly oscillator 2's
coupling pair is driven by oscillator 1.

Write KCL at $X_{1}$ in small signal.
With $v_{x1},v_{y1}$ :

$$\frac{v_{x1}}{sL}+sCv_{x1}+g_{SS}v_{y1}+g_{1}v_{gT1}=0$$

where $v_{gT1}$ is the gate voltage of the left
coupling device. The $g_{SS}v_{y1}$ is the drain
current of the cross device whose gate is on $Y_{1}$.
The source nodes are virtual ground for differential
signals.

Similarly at $Y_{1}$ :

$$\frac{v_{y1}}{sL}+sCv_{y1}+g_{SS}v_{x1}+g_{1}v_{gT4}=0$$

Subtract :

$$\left(\frac1{sL}+sC-g_{SS}\right)(v_{x1}-v_{y1})
+g_{1}(v_{gT1}-v_{gT4})=0 .$$

I.e.

$$(Y_{s}-g_{SS})V_{1}+g_{1}V_{c1}=0$$

where $Y_{s}=1/sL+sC$ plus tank loss,
and $V_{c1}=v_{gT1}-v_{gT4}$ is the differential
drive to the coupling pair from oscillator 2.

Similarly

$$(Y_{s}-g_{SS})V_{2}+g_{1}V_{c2}=0$$

where $V_{c2}$ is the differential drive to
oscillator 2's coupling pair from oscillator 1.

Follow the inter-oscillator wiring. One way is
straight, the other way is crossed, the X in the
middle. Hence to within an overall sign

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{c1} &= -V_{2}\\
V_{c2} &= +V_{1}
\end{aligned}$$

i.e. one injection is in phase, the other is anti
phase. Then

$$\begin{aligned}
(Y_{s}-g_{SS})V_{1}-g_{1}V_{2}&=0\\
(Y_{s}-g_{SS})V_{2}+g_{1}V_{1}&=0
\end{aligned}$$

Non-trivial $V_{1},V_{2}$ iff

$$(Y_{s}-g_{SS})^{2}+g_{1}^{2}=0$$

i.e.

$$Y_{s}-g_{SS}= \pm jg_{1} .$$

Put $Y_{s}=G_{p}+j(C\omega-1/L\omega)$ on
$s=j\omega$. In steady state, with effective
large signal $g_{m}$,

$$G_{p}-g_{SS,eff}+j\Bigl(C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}\Bigr)
= \pm jg_{1,eff} .$$

Hence

$$g_{SS,eff}\approx G_{p}$$

the core pair cancels tank loss, and

$$C\omega-\frac1{L\omega}= \pm g_{1,eff} .$$

The eigenvectors satisfy $V_{2}= \pm jV_{1}$;
the two tanks oscillate $90^{\circ}$ apart.

In particular for weak coupling,

$$\omega_{osc}^{2}+\mp\frac{g_{1,eff}}{C}\omega_{osc}
-\frac1{LC}\approx 0$$

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}\pm\frac{g_{1,eff}}{2C}$$

where

$$\omega_{0}=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}}$$

is the tank resonance. $\Delta\omega/\omega_{0}
\approx (g_{1}/g_{SS})/2Q$ is normally $\ll 1$.

To first order the circuit oscillates at the $LC$
resonance of one side to ground,

$$f_{osc}\approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_{tot}}}$$

in quadrature.

  $Q$ at
$$
\omega_{0}=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}}\qquad 
f_{0}=\frac1{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} .
$$

$$
X_{1}= {\rm Re}\,A_{1}e^{j\omega t},\qquad Y_{1}=-X_{1},\qquad
X_{2}= {\rm Re}\,A_{2}e^{j\omega t},\qquad Y_{2}=-X_{2}
$$
for the differential oscillation.  KCL at e.g. $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$,
with $g_{m}$ the (large signal, fundamental) transconductance of
the main pair and $g_{mc}$ that of the coupling pair, is

$$\begin{aligned}
\Bigl[G_{p}-g_{m}+j\Bigl(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\Bigr)\Bigr]A_{1}
      -g_{mc}A_{2}&=0\\
g_{mc}A_{1}+
\Bigl[G_{p}-g_{m}+j\Bigl(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\Bigr)\Bigr]A_{2}&=0
\end{aligned}$$
the sign change in the coupling term being the cross connection
in one of the two coupling paths in the figure.  Hence, with
$D=G_{p}-g_{m}+j(\omega C-1/\omega L)$,

$$
D^{2}+g_{mc}^{2}=0,\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad D=\pm jg_{mc},
\qquad \frac{A_{2}}{A_{1}}=\pm j .
$$

$A_{2}=\pm jA_{1}$ is quadrature between the two cores.  The real
part, $g_{m}=G_{p}=1/R_{p}$, is the ordinary amplitude condition;
the coupling current, being in quadrature with the voltage of
its own core, contributes no negative resistance to first order.
The imaginary part must be supplied by a detuned tank,

$$
\;\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}= \pm g_{mc}\;
$$

i.e. the $QVCO$ does not oscillate exactly at $\omega_{0}$.
In closed form, with $g_{mc}$ the effective coupling $g_{m}$,

$$
\omega_{\pm}= \omega_{0}
\Bigl[\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}\pm\alpha\Bigr],\qquad 
\alpha=\frac{g_{mc}}{2\omega_{0}C}\;,
$$
the two signs being the two quadrature modes, $X_{2}Y_{2}$ leading
or lagging $X_{1}Y_{1}$ by $90^{\circ}$.

For the usual high $Q$, hard switched, operation
$g_{m,{\rm eff}}=1/R_{p}$ and the fundamental coupling current is
in the ratio $I_{1}/I_{SS}$ to the main current, so

$\;\omega C-1/\omega L\approx2C(\omega-\omega_{0})$,

$$
\;\omega_{osc}\;\approx\;
\omega_{0}\pm\frac{g_{mc,{\rm eff}}}{2C}
\;\approx\;
\omega_{0}\left[\,1\pm\frac{1}{2Q}\,\frac{I_{1}}{I_{SS}}\right]\;
$$

$$
\,f_{osc}\approx f_{0}\left(1\pm\frac{I_{1}}{2QI_{SS}}\right),\qquad 
      f_{0}=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\,  .
$$

For normal values $I_{1}\lesssim I_{SS}$, $Q\sim5\!-\!10$, the split
is only a few percent.  To the accuracy usually required the
quadrature oscillator therefore runs at the tank resonance
$1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$, the coupling merely detuning it by
$\pm (f_{0}/2Q)(I_{1}/I_{SS})$ according as it locks in the

Each of the two stacked blocks is a **cross‑coupled differential pair** (the inner pair, biased by $I_1$, is a regenerative latch; the outer pair, biased by $I_{SS}$, is the input/switching pair of the block). The two blocks are cross‑connected so that the signal loops $X_1/Y_1 \rightarrow$ block 2 $\rightarrow X_2/Y_2 \rightarrow$ block 1, giving a closed positive‑feedback (differential) ring.

The key element for *frequency* is the **on‑chip inductor from each drain node to $V_{DD}$** (i.e. to AC ground). Together with the small‑signal capacitance that exists at that node, each drain node ($X_1, Y_1$ and $X_2, Y_2$) forms a **parallel LC tank**. The cross‑coupled pairs (and the second block, which only adds loop gain / relaxes the $g_m$ requirement) supply the **negative resistance** that cancels the tank loss and starts the oscillation. The nodes oscillate 180° out of phase (differential mode).

So the bias currents $I_{SS}$ and $I_1$ set the **bias point, the negative‑resistance value (start‑up condition) and the amplitude**, but they do **not** set the frequency. The frequency is set by the tank.

## Estimated oscillation frequency

To first order the circuit rings at the resonant frequency of each drain‑node tank:

$$\boxed{\,f_{osc} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_{node}}}\,}$$

where

* $L$ = the inductor connected from the node to $V_{DD}$, and
* $C_{node}$ = total small‑signal capacitance from that drain node to AC ground = the drain‑to‑bulk capacitances of the devices tied to the node plus layout/stray parasitics (the gate‑drain capacitances add a Miller‑type contribution; in the differential mode part of it cancels). On silicon this is typically on the order of a few ×10 fF to a few ×100 fF.

**Start‑up (context, not frequency):** the differential negative resistance presented by the cross‑coupled pairs, $R_{neg}\approx -2/g_{m,cross}$ (with $g_{m,cross}$ set by $I_1$, aided by the second block set by $I_{SS}$), must satisfy $|R_{neg}| < R_{tank}$ so the amplitude builds. This determines *whether* it oscillates and the peak‑to‑peak voltage, not $f_{osc}$.

## Numerical ballpark (no values were given in the figure)

Because $L$ and $C_{node}$ are not specified, a number requires assuming typical on‑chip values:

| $L$ | $C_{node}$ | $f_{osc}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ |
|-----|-----------|------------------------------------------|
| 1 nH | 50 fF | ≈ 22 GHz |
| 2 nH | 100 fF | ≈ 11 GHz |
| 5 nH | 200 fF | ≈ 5 GHz |
| 10 nH | 300 fF | ≈ 2.9 GHz |

Hence, with realistic on‑chip inductors the oscillator operates in the **GHz range**, and the governing estimate is $f_{osc}\simeq 1/(2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_{node}})$, independent of $I_{SS}$ and $I_1$ (which control start‑up and amplitude).

**In short:** it is an LC (tank) oscillator; the oscillation frequency is the resonance of each inductive load with the node capacitance, $f_{osc}\approx 1/(2\pi\sqrt{L\,C_{node}})$, while the bias currents only ensure the negative‑resistance start‑up condition.
